title: One day (109–115)
hook: better one day seeing how things arise and pass than a hundred years without seeing it

segments.voice: Yesterday, the greatest conquest: winning over yourself, a victory no one can undo. Today, the end of the thousands chapter.

Some single days stay clearer than whole years. A wedding. A birth. The day of a diagnosis. A day walking somewhere new, when the light, the food and the faces all seemed to glow. And some years slide by and leave almost nothing behind: the commute, the inbox, the same dinner. Length and life aren't the same thing. The last verses of chapter eight make that point six times over, then name what makes a day worth more than a century.
screen: `ONE DAY YOU REMEMBER.` → `YEARS THAT LEFT NOTHING.` → `LENGTH ISN'T LIFE.`

segments.voice: Verse one hundred ten, in Müller's English: someone may live a hundred years, careless and unrestrained, but “a life of one day is better if a man is virtuous and reflecting.” The next verses repeat the shape. A hundred years without wisdom, or one day with it. A hundred years idle and weak, or one day of real effort. Then verse one hundred thirteen: someone may live a hundred years without seeing how things begin and end, but “a life of one day is better if a man sees beginning and end.” In Pali, udayabbaya: arising and passing away. In the Theravada tradition it names a stage of insight practice: seeing, not just knowing, that every thought, feeling, sound and moment comes up and goes. The commentary ties this verse to a woman named Patacara. In a single terrible stretch, the story says, she lost her husband, both her children, her parents and her brother. She came to the Buddha out of her mind with grief, and he calmed her and taught her. Her own verses, preserved in the collection of the early nuns, describe the turning point: washing her feet, she watched the water run down the slope. The commentary adds that it ran a short way, then farther, then farther still, and that she saw in it lives ending young, in middle age, and old. That same night, her verses say, her mind was freed. The chapter's last two verses say the same of seeing the deathless and the highest teaching. Not because the years don't matter. Because a single day, lived awake, is where seeing happens.
screen: `A HUNDRED YEARS, OR ONE DAY.` · `UDAYABBAYA — ARISING AND PASSING.` · `PATACARA AND THE WATER.` · `WHERE SEEING HAPPENS.` · then, large: `ONE DAY, AWAKE.`

segments.voice: Watch one breath begin and end, then the next. Listen for a sound and notice where it starts and where it fades; feel a sensation in the hands or feet arise, change and pass. Don't hold on to any of it: just watch things come up and go, like water running off onto the ground.
One day. Better one day seeing how things arise and pass away than a hundred years without seeing it.
Your line: one day, awake. Everything you notice has a beginning and an end. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In insight meditation, practitioners watch sensations, sounds and thoughts arise and pass away, and the story of the nun Patacara is told as an example of this seeing bringing freedom from grief.

fork.setup: you're Patacara, washing your feet. you pour water; it runs a short way, then farther, then farther still. what did she see?
options: how lives come and go, like the water.

fork.reveal: in the commentary, the water's short and long runs showed her how beings die young, in middle age or old; her own verses say her mind was freed that night.

what a scholar hears: verse 113's 'apassam udayabbayam' names insight into arising and passing (udayabbaya-nana); Patacara's verses are Therigatha 112–116.
recall: the wise one, who welcomes correction

chat.says: Is it true one awake day is worth more than a hundred careless years? How?
options: Yes: the verse says one day seeing things arise and pass beats a century without seeing it.
Yes, because a long life is a burden, so the verse says a shorter life is the better one.
Only for monks; the verse says ordinary people need the full hundred years to learn it.
chat.meaning: Verse 113: better one day seeing beginning and end, arising and passing away, than a hundred years blind to it. Length and life aren't the same.
